# async_dup - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/async-dup/

## Expand description

Duplicate an async I/O handle.

This crate provides two tools, [ Arc](https://docs.rs/struct.Arc.html) and

[:](https://docs.rs/struct.Mutex.html)

`Mutex`- `Arc`- `AsyncRead`- `AsyncWrite`- `AsyncSeek`
- A reference to `Mutex``AsyncRead``AsyncWrite``AsyncSeek`

Wrap an async I/O handle in [ Arc](https://docs.rs/struct.Arc.html) or

[to clone it or share among tasks.](https://docs.rs/struct.Mutex.html)

`Mutex`[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

Clone an async I/O handle:

```
use async_dup::Arc;
use futures::io;
use smol::Async;
use std::net::TcpStream;
// A client that echoes messages back to the server.
let stream = Async::<TcpStream>::connect(([127, 0, 0, 1], 8000)).await?;
// Create two handles to the stream.
let reader = Arc::new(stream);
let mut writer = reader.clone();
// Echo data received from the reader back into the writer.
io::copy(reader, &mut writer).await?;
```
Share an async I/O handle:

```
use async_dup::Mutex;
use futures::io;
use futures::prelude::*;
// Reads data from a stream and echoes it back.
async fn echo(stream: impl AsyncRead + AsyncWrite + Unpin) -> io::Result<u64> {
    let stream = Mutex::new(stream);
    io::copy(&stream, &mut &stream).await
}
```
## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Arc](https://docs.rs/struct.Arc.html)
- A reference-counted pointer that implements async I/O traits.
- [Mutex](https://docs.rs/struct.Mutex.html)
- A mutex that implements async I/O traits.
- [Mutex](https://docs.rs/struct.MutexGuard.html)- Guard
- A guard that releases the mutex when dropped.

# async-dup 1.2.4 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/async-dup/latest

# async-dup

Duplicate an async I/O handle.

This crate provides two tools, `Arc` and `Mutex`:

- `Arc`implements- `AsyncRead`,- `AsyncWrite`, and- `AsyncSeek`if a reference to the inner type does.
- A reference to `Mutex`implements`AsyncRead`,`AsyncWrite`, and`AsyncSeek`if the inner type does.

Wrap an async I/O handle in `Arc` or `Mutex` to clone it or share among tasks.

## Examples

Clone an async I/O handle:

```
use Arc;
use io;
use Async;
use TcpStream;
// A client that echoes messages back to the server.
let stream = connect.await?;
// Create two handles to the stream.
let reader = new;
let mut writer = reader.clone;
// Echo data received from the reader back into the writer.
copy.await?;
```
Share an async I/O handle:

```
use Mutex;
use io;
use *;
// Reads data from a stream and echoes it back.
async
```

# async_lock - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/async-lock/^3.1.0/

## Expand description

Async synchronization primitives.

This crate provides the following primitives:

- `Barrier`
- `Mutex`
- `RwLock`
- `Semaphore`

[§](https://docs.rs#relationship-with-stdsync)Relationship with `std::sync`

In general, you should consider using [ std::sync](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/sync/index.html) types over types from this crate.

There are two primary use cases for types from this crate:

- You need to use a synchronization primitive in a `no_std`environment.
- You need to hold a lock across an `.await`point. (Holding an`std::sync``.await`will make your future non-`Send`, and is also highly likely to cause deadlocks.)

If you already use `libstd` and you aren’t holding locks across await points (there is a
Clippy lint called [ await_holding_lock](https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-clippy/stable/index.html#/await_holding_lock) that emits warnings for this scenario), you should
consider

[instead of this crate. Those types are optimized for the currently running operating system, are less complex and are generally much faster.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/sync/index.html)

`std::sync`In contrast, `async-lock`’s notification system uses `std::sync::Mutex` under the hood if
the `std` feature is enabled, and will fall back to a significantly slower strategy if it is
not. So, there are few cases where `async-lock` is a win for performance over [ std::sync](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/sync/index.html).

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [futures](https://docs.rs/futures/index.html)
- Named futures for use with `async_lock`primitives.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Barrier](https://docs.rs/struct.Barrier.html)
- A counter to synchronize multiple tasks at the same time.
- [Barrier](https://docs.rs/struct.BarrierWaitResult.html)- Wait - Result
- Returned by `Barrier::wait()`
- [Mutex](https://docs.rs/struct.Mutex.html)
- An async mutex.
- [Mutex](https://docs.rs/struct.MutexGuard.html)- Guard
- A guard that releases the mutex when dropped.
- [Mutex](https://docs.rs/struct.MutexGuardArc.html)- Guard - Arc
- An owned guard that releases the mutex when dropped.
- [Once](https://docs.rs/struct.OnceCell.html)- Cell
- A memory location that can be written to at most once.
- [RwLock](https://docs.rs/struct.RwLock.html)
- An async reader-writer lock.
- [RwLock](https://docs.rs/struct.RwLockReadGuard.html)- Read - Guard
- A guard that releases the read lock when dropped.
- [RwLock](https://docs.rs/struct.RwLockReadGuardArc.html)- Read - Guard - Arc
- An owned, reference-counting guard that releases the read lock when dropped.
- [RwLock](https://docs.rs/struct.RwLockUpgradableReadGuard.html)- Upgradable - Read - Guard
- A guard that releases the upgradable read lock when dropped.
- [RwLock](https://docs.rs/struct.RwLockUpgradableReadGuardArc.html)- Upgradable - Read - Guard - Arc
- An owned, reference-counting guard that releases the upgradable read lock when dropped.
- [RwLock](https://docs.rs/struct.RwLockWriteGuard.html)- Write - Guard
- A guard that releases the write lock when dropped.
- [RwLock](https://docs.rs/struct.RwLockWriteGuardArc.html)- Write - Guard - Arc
- An owned, reference-counted guard that releases the write lock when dropped.
- [Semaphore](https://docs.rs/struct.Semaphore.html)
- A counter for limiting the number of concurrent operations.
- [Semaphore](https://docs.rs/struct.SemaphoreGuard.html)- Guard
- A guard that releases the acquired permit.
- [Semaphore](https://docs.rs/struct.SemaphoreGuardArc.html)- Guard - Arc
- An owned guard that releases the acquired permit.

# futures_io - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/futures-io/^0.3.5/

## Expand description

Asynchronous I/O

This crate contains the `AsyncRead`, `AsyncWrite`, `AsyncSeek`, and
`AsyncBufRead` traits, the asynchronous analogs to
`std::io::{Read, Write, Seek, BufRead}`. The primary difference is
that these traits integrate with the asynchronous task system.

All items of this library are only available when the `std` feature of this
library is activated, and it is activated by default.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use io::`- [Error](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/io/error/struct.Error.html);
- `pub use io::`- [ErrorKind](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/io/error/enum.ErrorKind.html);
- `pub use io::`- [IoSlice](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/io/io_slice/struct.IoSlice.html);
- `pub use io::`- [IoSliceMut](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/io/io_slice/struct.IoSliceMut.html);
- `pub use io::`- [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/io/error/type.Result.html);
- `pub use io::`- [SeekFrom](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/io/enum.SeekFrom.html);

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Async](https://docs.rs/trait.AsyncBufRead.html)- BufRead - `std`
- Read bytes asynchronously.
- [Async](https://docs.rs/trait.AsyncRead.html)- Read - `std`
- Read bytes asynchronously.
- [Async](https://docs.rs/trait.AsyncSeek.html)- Seek - `std`
- Seek bytes asynchronously.
- [Async](https://docs.rs/trait.AsyncWrite.html)- Write - `std`
- Write bytes asynchronously.

# futures - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/futures/^0.3.5/

## Expand description

Abstractions for asynchronous programming.

This crate provides a number of core abstractions for writing asynchronous code:

- [Futures](https://docs.rs/future/index.html)are single eventual values produced by asynchronous computations. Some programming languages (e.g. JavaScript) call this concept “promise”.
- [Streams](https://docs.rs/stream/index.html)represent a series of values produced asynchronously.
- [Sinks](https://docs.rs/sink/index.html)provide support for asynchronous writing of data.
- [Executors](https://docs.rs/executor/index.html)are responsible for running asynchronous tasks.

The crate also contains abstractions for [asynchronous I/O](https://docs.rs/io/index.html) and
[cross-task communication](https://docs.rs/channel/index.html).

Underlying all of this is the *task system*, which is a form of lightweight
threading. Large asynchronous computations are built up using futures,
streams and sinks, and then spawned as independent tasks that are run to
completion, but *do not block* the thread running them.

The following example describes how the task system context is built and used within macros and keywords such as async and await!.

```
fn main() {
    let pool = ThreadPool::new().expect("Failed to build pool");
    let (tx, rx) = mpsc::unbounded::<i32>();
    // Create a future by an async block, where async is responsible for an
    // implementation of Future. At this point no executor has been provided
    // to this future, so it will not be running.
    let fut_values = async {
        // Create another async block, again where the Future implementation
        // is generated by async. Since this is inside of a parent async block,
        // it will be provided with the executor of the parent block when the parent
        // block is executed.
        //
        // This executor chaining is done by Future::poll whose second argument
        // is a std::task::Context. This represents our executor, and the Future
        // implemented by this async block can be polled using the parent async
        // block's executor.
        let fut_tx_result = async move {
            (0..100).for_each(|v| {
                tx.unbounded_send(v).expect("Failed to send");
            })
        };
        // Use the provided thread pool to spawn the generated future
        // responsible for transmission
        pool.spawn_ok(fut_tx_result);
        let fut_values = rx
            .map(|v| v * 2)
            .collect();
        // Use the executor provided to this async block to wait for the
        // future to complete.
        fut_values.await
    };
    // Actually execute the above future, which will invoke Future::poll and
    // subsequently chain appropriate Future::poll and methods needing executors
    // to drive all futures. Eventually fut_values will be driven to completion.
    let values: Vec<i32> = executor::block_on(fut_values);
    println!("Values={:?}", values);
}
```
The majority of examples and code snippets in this crate assume that they are inside an async block as written above.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [join](https://docs.rs/macro.join.html)- `async-await`
- Polls multiple futures simultaneously, returning a tuple of all results once complete.
- [pending](https://docs.rs/macro.pending.html)- `async-await`
- A macro which yields to the event loop once.
- [pin_mut](https://docs.rs/macro.pin_mut.html)
- Pins a value on the stack.
- [poll](https://docs.rs/macro.poll.html)- `async-await`
- A macro which returns the result of polling a future once within the
current `async`context.
- [ready](https://docs.rs/macro.ready.html)
- Extracts the successful type of `Poll<T>`.
- [select](https://docs.rs/macro.select.html)- `async-await`and- `std`
- Polls multiple futures and streams simultaneously, executing the branch
for the future that finishes first. If multiple futures are ready,
one will be pseudo-randomly selected at runtime. Futures directly
passed to `select!`must be`Unpin`and implement`FusedFuture`.
- [select_](https://docs.rs/macro.select_biased.html)- biased - `async-await`
- Polls multiple futures and streams simultaneously, executing the branch
for the future that finishes first. Unlike `select!``select_biased!`must be`Unpin`and implement`FusedFuture`.
- [stream_](https://docs.rs/macro.stream_select.html)- select - `async-await`and- `std`
- Combines several streams, all producing the same `Item`type, into one stream. This is similar to`select_all`but does not require the streams to all be the same type. It also keeps the streams inline, and does not require`Box<dyn Stream>`s to be allocated. Streams passed to this macro must be`Unpin`.
- [try_](https://docs.rs/macro.try_join.html)- join - `async-await`
- Polls multiple futures simultaneously, resolving to a `Result`

# smol - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/smol/^1/

## Expand description

A small and fast async runtime.

This crate simply re-exports other smaller async crates (see the source).

To use tokio-based libraries with smol, apply the [ async-compat](https://docs.rs/async-compat) adapter to futures and I/O
types.

Connect to an HTTP website, make a GET request, and pipe the response to the standard output:

```
use smol::{io, net, prelude::*, Unblock};
fn main() -> io::Result<()> {
    smol::block_on(async {
        let mut stream = net::TcpStream::connect("example.com:80").await?;
        let req = b"GET / HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: example.com\r\nConnection: close\r\n\r\n";
        stream.write_all(req).await?;
        let mut stdout = Unblock::new(std::io::stdout());
        io::copy(stream, &mut stdout).await?;
        Ok(())
    })
}
```
There’s a lot more in the [examples](https://github.com/smol-rs/smol/tree/master/examples) directory.

---

# async_dup - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/async-dup/latest/target-redirect/async_dup/

## Expand description

Duplicate an async I/O handle.

This crate provides two tools, [ Arc](https://docs.rs/struct.Arc.html) and

[:](https://docs.rs/struct.Mutex.html)

`Mutex`- `Arc`- `AsyncRead`- `AsyncWrite`- `AsyncSeek`
- A reference to `Mutex``AsyncRead``AsyncWrite``AsyncSeek`

Wrap an async I/O handle in [ Arc](https://docs.rs/struct.Arc.html) or

[to clone it or share among tasks.](https://docs.rs/struct.Mutex.html)

`Mutex`[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

Clone an async I/O handle:

```
use async_dup::Arc;
use futures::io;
use smol::Async;
use std::net::TcpStream;
// A client that echoes messages back to the server.
let stream = Async::<TcpStream>::connect(([127, 0, 0, 1], 8000)).await?;
// Create two handles to the stream.
let reader = Arc::new(stream);
let mut writer = reader.clone();
// Echo data received from the reader back into the writer.
io::copy(reader, &mut writer).await?;
```
Share an async I/O handle:

```
use async_dup::Mutex;
use futures::io;
use futures::prelude::*;
// Reads data from a stream and echoes it back.
async fn echo(stream: impl AsyncRead + AsyncWrite + Unpin) -> io::Result<u64> {
    let stream = Mutex::new(stream);
    io::copy(&stream, &mut &stream).await
}
```

# About Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/about

Docs.rs is an
            [open source](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs)
            documentation host for crates of the
            [Rust Programming Language](https://www.rust-lang.org/).
            All libraries published to [crates.io](https://crates.io)
            are documented. If you just published a crate, your crate is likely
            still in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

            The source code of Docs.rs is available on
            [GitHub](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs). If
            you ever encounter an issue, don't hesitate to report it! (And
            thanks in advance!)

Currently running Docs.rs version is: **0.0.0 (964c90a45859fd8f9076e3cbe58470a5a4f4d4f7 2026-07-01 )**

Summaries of the documentation build processes [are available at /releases/](https://docs.rs/releases).

            JavaScript in support of documentation is allowed but not guaranteed to work on docs.rs. What that
            means: If you write documentation that inlines some JavaScript (like
            [KaTeX](https://katex.org/)), that's allowed, and
            will probably work today but may break in the future.

However, it's not allowed to put JavaScript or other content in docs published on docs.rs for the purpose of tracking visitors. For instance, adding Google Analytics scripts, tracking pixels, or site verification for services like Google Search Console. Crates that do this will have the relevant versions removed and may be blocked from docs.rs.

            Docs.rs is run and maintained by the [Docs.rs team](https://www.rust-lang.org/governance/teams/dev-tools#team-docs-rs).
            You can find us in #t-docs-rs on [Zulip](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/stream/356853-t-docs-rs).

# Builds

Source: https://docs.rs/about/builds

Docs.rs automatically builds documentation for crates released on [crates.io](https://crates.io/).
                It may take a while to build your crate, depending on how many crates are in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

                All crates are built in a sandbox using the nightly release of the Rust compiler.
                The current version in use is `rustc 1.98.0-nightly (c397dae80 2026-07-02)`.

                The README displayed on docs.rs follows Cargo’s `package.readme` rules.
                If `readme` is not set, docs.rs will look for `README.md`, `README.txt`, or `README` in the crate root.
                Set `readme = "path/to/file"` to use a custom file, `readme = true` to use `README.md`, or `readme = false` to disable the README.

                To recognize Docs.rs from your Rust code, you can test for the `docsrs` cfg, e.g.:

```
```
                To recognize Docs.rs from `build.rs` files, you can test for the environment variable `DOCS_RS`, e.g.:

`if var.is_ok `
              All targets other than `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` are cross-compiled. For implementation reasons, this is unlikely to change for the foreseeable future.

                You can configure how your crate is built by adding [package metadata](https://docs.rs/metadata) to your `Cargo.toml`, e.g.:

```
[]
 = ["--cfg", "my_cfg"]
```
`#[cfg(my_cfg)]` (not to be confused with `#[cfg(doc)]`) can be used for conditional compilation.
                This approach is also useful for setting
                When you start using docs.rs metadata or `#[cfg(docsrs)]` in your code, you might run into issues
                where your code builds fine locally but fails on docs.rs.
                To avoid this, you can add [ cargo docs-rs](https://github.com/dtolnay/cargo-docs-rs) to
                your test-suite.
                While it doesn't perfectly replicate our build environment, it can catch many common issues.

                The Docs.rs [README](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/blob/master/README.md#build-subcommand) describes how to build
                unpublished crate documentation locally using the same build environment as the Docs.rs build agent.

                Missing dependencies are a common reason for failed builds.
                Docs.rs dependencies are managed through
                [crates-build-env](https://github.com/rust-lang/crates-build-env).
                See [Forge](https://forge.rust-lang.org/docs-rs/add-dependencies.html) for how to add a dependency.

                Most of the sandbox is a read-only file system, including the source directory of your crate and its dependencies.
                If your `build.rs` generates files that are relevant for documentation, consider writing to the
                [cargo output directory](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/environment-variables.html#environment-variables-cargo-sets-for-crates),
                passed in the environment variable `OUT_DIR`.

All the builds are executed inside a sandbox with limited resources. The current limits are:

| Available RAM | 6.44 GB |
| Maximum rustdoc execution time | 15m |
| Maximum size of a build log | 102.4 kB |
| Network access | blocked |
| Maximum number of build targets | 10 |

                If your build fails because it hit one of these limits, please
                [open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose)
                to get them increased for your crate.
                Since our build agent has finite resources, we have to consider each case individually. However, there are a few general policies:

If your crate fails to build for a reason not listed here, you can rebuild it from [crates.io](https://crates.io) website as you can see below:

Or you can [file an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues) if you think it's a **docs.rs** issue.

---

# Metadata

Source: https://docs.rs/about/metadata

You can customize docs.rs builds by defining `[package.metadata.docs.rs]`
		table in your crates' `Cargo.toml`.

The available configuration flags you can customize are:

```
[]
 = "test"
[]
# Features to pass to Cargo (default: [])
 = ["feature1", "feature2"]
# Whether to pass `--all-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Whether to pass `--no-default-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Target to test build on, used as the default landing page (default: "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu")
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
 = "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu"
# Targets to build (default: see below)
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
#
# Default targets:
# - x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - aarch64-apple-darwin
# - x86_64-pc-windows-msvc
# - aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - i686-pc-windows-msvc
#
# Set this to `[]` to only build the default target.
#
# If `default-target` is unset, the first element of `targets` is treated as the default target.
# Otherwise, these `targets` are built in addition to the default target.
# If both `default-target` and `targets` are unset,
#   all tier-one targets will be built and `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` will be used as the default target.
 = ["aarch64-apple-darwin", "x86_64-pc-windows-msvc"]
# If you want to instead add another target without overwriting the default ones:
 = ["i686-apple-darwin"]
# Additional `RUSTFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustc-arg"]
# Additional `RUSTDOCFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustdoc-arg"]
# List of command line arguments for `cargo`.
#
# These cannot be a subcommand, they may only be options.
 = ["-Z", "build-std"]
```

# Shorthand URLs

Source: https://docs.rs/about/redirections

Docs.rs uses semver to parse URLs. You can use this feature to access
            crates' documentation easily. Example of URL redirections for
            `clap` crate:

| URL | Redirects to documentation of |
|---|---|
| [docs.rs/clap](https://docs.rs/clap) | Latest version of clap |
| [docs.rs/clap::Command](https://docs.rs/clap::Command) | Latest version of clap, and search for "Command" within the crate |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2) | 2.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2.9](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2.9) | 2.9.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/2.9.3](https://docs.rs/clap/2.9.3) | 2.9.3 version (you don't need `=`unlike semver) |
| [docs.rs/clap/*](https://docs.rs/clap/*) | Latest version of this page (if it still exists). "latest" or "newest" work as well as `*`. |

---

# Download

Source: https://docs.rs/about/download

docs.rs stores the `rustdoc` output in a ZIP file.

                These archives can be used as a base for further processing of
                the documentation for offline readers like Dash or Zeal.
                **They are not directly usable for offline documentation.**

The download is possible for specific or semantic versions:

But also viaTo unpack the ZIP file you need any zip utility that supports PKZIP version 4.6 and BZIP2 & Deflate compression.

The archives will contain all the documentation HTML files for all targets and CSS/JS assets that are specific to the build. The default target will be found at the root, and other targets each in its own subfolder.

                Docs.rs is running rustdoc with `--static-root-path "/-/rustdoc.static/"`,
                which leads to all references to static assets breaking if they are not
                available under that path. Older builds used `--static-root-path "/"`, which
                means you will have to handle both.

                Since we're also adding `--emit=invocation-specific` to our build
                the archives will *not* contain any static assets that are specific to the
                toolchain. For now these will have to be downloaded file-by-file directly
                from docs.rs.

---

# Rustdoc JSON

Source: https://docs.rs/about/rustdoc-json

docs.rs builds & hosts the [ rustdoc JSON](https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustdoc/unstable-features.html#json-output) output.

This structured version of the documentation can be used for inspecting the docs and types of the crate in a programmatic way.

                The JSON file you're downloading might have been built with an older version of `rustdoc`
                so you might have to check the `format_version` attribute to determine how to parse the structure.
                The [ rustdoc-types](https://docs.rs/rustdoc-types/) crate helps with this.

**
                We started building rustdoc JSON on 2025-05-23. So any release before that won't have a download
                available until our rebuilds reached that release.
            **

                The download URLs can be generic or specific, depending on what you need. In case of rebuilds we
                also keep old format versions around. **Until we rebuilt all releases, we might return
                a `404 NOT FOUND` for some.**

By default we use `zstd` compression, which is more space efficient and faster to decompress. For more limited environments we also started supporting `gzip` compression. You can receive gzip by adding `.gz` to the given URL.

Here some URL examples you can use.

| URL | Redirects to JSON download of |
|---|---|
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json) | latest version, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz) | latest version, default target, latest format-version, gzip compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42) | latest version, default target, format-version 42 |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json.zst](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json.zst) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version, zstd compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json) | latest version, windows target, latest format-version |

# datum_net - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/datum-net/0.9.0/datum_net/

## Expand description

Network sources and sinks for Datum streams.

`datum-net` is the network satellite crate for the Datum family. It provides
TLS-wrapped TCP sources and sinks through [ TokioTls](https://docs.rs/tls/struct.TokioTls.html) plus UDP datagram
sources, sinks, and flows through

[, and QUIC endpoint/stream helpers through](https://docs.rs/udp/struct.TokioUdp.html)

`TokioUdp`[. Connection lifecycle helpers add timeout, retry, and explicit half-close affordances for client connection flows.](https://docs.rs/quic/struct.TokioQuic.html)

`TokioQuic`## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use connection::`- [Connection](https://docs.rs/connection/struct.Connection.html);
- `pub use connection::`- [ConnectionLifecycleExt](https://docs.rs/connection/trait.ConnectionLifecycleExt.html);
- `pub use connection::`- [ConnectionSettings](https://docs.rs/connection/struct.ConnectionSettings.html);
- `pub use connection::`- [RetryPolicy](https://docs.rs/connection/struct.RetryPolicy.html);
- `pub use quic::`- [DEFAULT_CHUNK_SIZE](https://docs.rs/quic/constant.DEFAULT_CHUNK_SIZE.html)as QUIC_DEFAULT_CHUNK_SIZE;

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [connection](https://docs.rs/connection/index.html)
- Connection lifecycle utilities for `datum-net`transports.
- [quic](https://docs.rs/quic/index.html)
- QUIC endpoints, connections, and bidirectional byte streams.
- [stream_](https://docs.rs/stream_ref/index.html)- ref
- Remote StreamRefs carriers.
- [tls](https://docs.rs/tls/index.html)
- TLS-wrapped TCP sources and sinks.

# datum - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/datum-core/0.9.0/datum/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#datum)Datum

🪼 - Just “Stream” anything :]

Datum is a Rust stream processing library scaffolded around Ractor actors and a push-based stream abstraction. The compatibility target is Akka/Pekko Streams Typed API shape and behavior, with Rust-native ownership, async, and benchmarking constraints.

[§](https://docs.rs#install)Install

Add Datum to your project from crates.io:

`cargo add datum-core`Or in `Cargo.toml`:

```
[dependencies]
datum-core = "0.9"
```

Note:The package is published as`datum-core`(the name`datum`is taken on crates.io), but the import path stays`use datum::…`— the crate’s library name is`datum`.

To track an unreleased commit instead:

```
[dependencies]
datum-core = { git = "https://github.com/Aethergrids/Datum", tag = "v0.9.0" }
```
[§](https://docs.rs#upstream-references)Upstream References

- Ractor crate: `0.15.13`
- Optional Ractor cluster crate: `0.15.13`, enabled with`--features cluster`
- Akka source submodule: `third_party/akka`, tracking upstream`main`and pinned in this repository at commit`58f1f6db2e505e87f5dc115ee9476833872e7ae0`
- Latest stable Akka tag observed during setup: `v2.10.18`

[§](https://docs.rs#feature-highlights-v090)Feature highlights (v0.9.0)

- **Concurrency primitives**(- `datum::concurrent`) —- `Signal<T>`(latest-value state cell with a lock-free- `get()`and a coalesced change feed),- `Subscription<T>`(the same state cell with a lossless every-change feed),- `Channel<T>`(closeable bounded MPSC), and- `Topic<T>`(pub-sub broadcast with backpressure/sliding/dropping overflow policies). Benchmarked 4-way against FS2, ZIO, and Akka: every row beats the best JVM competitor on both wall-clock and CPU.
- **API ergonomics (additive, zero semantic change)**—- `use datum::prelude::*;`, terminal shortcuts (- `run_fold`/- `run_foreach`/- `run_reduce`),- `(0..n).into_source()`/- `Source::from(vec)`, the graph wiring DSL- `builder.wire(a.to(&b))`(with- `connect()`still first-class), and idiomatic- `try_*`fallible operators (- `try_map`,- `try_filter`, … —- `*_result`names deprecated).
- **Complete Akka Streams surface**— the linear DSL, GraphDSL with typed junctions and cycles, substreams, dynamic streams (kill switches, hubs), StreamRefs (same-process splice + remote transport via- `datum-net`), streaming IO, and IO adapters bridging to- `std::io::Read`/- `Write`.
- `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]`on the- `datum`crate itself; lock-free internals come from safe deps (- `crossbeam-queue`,- `arc-swap`).

[§](https://docs.rs#development)Development

```
cargo test
cargo check --benches
cargo bench --bench push_baseline
cargo bench --bench source_flow
cargo bench --bench materialization
cargo bench --bench graph
cargo bench --bench actor_ask
benches/actor_ask_compare/run.sh
```
```
use datum::prelude::*;
let sum = (0_u64..1_000)
    .into_source()
    .map(|item| item + 1)
    .filter(|item| item % 2 == 0)
    .run_fold(0_u64, |acc, item| acc + item)
    .unwrap()
    .wait()
    .unwrap();
assert_eq!(sum, 250_500);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#benchmarks)Benchmarks

Datum is benchmarked head-to-head against warmed Akka/Pekko Streams across eight core areas —
Source/Flow, materialization, graph/junctions, actor ask, dynamic streams, streaming IO, substreams,
and queues — plus network carriers (`datum-net`) and a 4-way concurrency-primitives comparison
against FS2, ZIO, and Akka. Honest per-path numbers (including any at-parity rows) are in the result
tables under `roadmap/benchmarks/`. The harness adds a `Datum CPU us/op` column on purpose: some
wins come partly from busy-spinning while a JVM parks — a real cost the wall-clock number hides.

Qualitative summary of the current state:

- **Fused linear path:**13–46x Akka (typed plan; all common sink shapes).
- **Junctions:**2.3–340x; typed kernels cover all major shapes;- **graph cycles**~29x.
- **Concurrency primitives (vs best of FS2/ZIO/Akka per row):**Channel MPSC ×1024 7.5x wall / 20.5x CPU; Signal reads ~ns-class (3.6–7.8x ZIO); Signal propagation ×1024 83x; Subscription lossless ×256 43x; Topic fanout ×1024 23x.
- **Remote StreamRefs (forced-remote Akka Artery-TCP, fair):**~9.9x faster wall, ~14.8x lower CPU, ~35x lower allocation; same-process splice ~6.5x.
- **Dynamic hubs:**MergeHub p16 ~16x (p1 ~0.46x — core materialization floor, documented); BroadcastHub 1.3–2x; PartitionHub 1.4–2.7x.
- **Queues:**source-queue backpressure ~985x; bounded queue ~parity wall with ~112x less allocation.
- **Actor ask:**~2.4–3x at p2–p4; allocation dominated by upstream Ractor boxing (~848 B/element, upstream-blocked).
- **Streaming IO adapters:**~7.4x on the round-trip scenario;- **materialization:**at parity.

Run a comparison (requires a JDK + `sbt`); each runner writes a rendered table under `target/<area>-comparison/`:

```
benches/source_flow_compare/run.sh
benches/materialization_compare/run.sh
benches/graph_compare/run.sh
benches/actor_ask_compare/run.sh
benches/dynamic_streams_compare/run.sh
benches/streaming_io_compare/run.sh
benches/substreams_compare/run.sh
```
Current result tables, the per-operator coverage matrix, and apples-to-apples caveats:

- `roadmap/benchmarks/source-flow.md`
- `roadmap/benchmarks/materialization.md`
- `roadmap/benchmarks/graph.md`
- `roadmap/benchmarks/actor-ask.md`
- `roadmap/benchmarks/dynamic-streams.md`
- `roadmap/benchmarks/streaming-io.md`
- `roadmap/benchmarks/substreams.md`
- `roadmap/M1-v0.1.0-foundation.md`— coverage matrix, optimization status & apples-to-apples caveats
- `roadmap/M4-v0.4.0-completeness-hardening.md`— M4 work packages and exit criteria

See [ roadmap/](https://docs.rs/roadmap/README.md) for the full milestone roadmap. User documentation is the published VitePress site (Cloudflare Pages);

`docs/` holds its source. `roadmap/` holds internal planning and benchmark records.## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [actor](https://docs.rs/actor/index.html)
- Actor interop: Ractor-backed stream bridges plus the remote StreamRefs seam.
- [concurrent](https://docs.rs/concurrent/index.html)
- Stream-native concurrency primitives.
- [context](https://docs.rs/context/index.html)
- Context-aware stream wrappers.
- [dynamic](https://docs.rs/dynamic/index.html)
- Dynamic stream controls and attachment points modeled after Akka Streams.
- [graph](https://docs.rs/graph/index.html)
- Runtime-checked graph, shape, port, and junction primitives.
- [io](https://docs.rs/io/index.html)
- Streaming I/O — file and TCP sources/sinks, byte framing, compression, and `std::io`bridges.
- [prelude](https://docs.rs/prelude/index.html)
- [queue](https://docs.rs/queue/index.html)
- Bounded and unbounded queues that bridge external producers into a Datum stream.
- [stream](https://docs.rs/stream/index.html)
- The linear Source/Flow/Sink DSL and the runtime that materializes it — Datum’s primary public surface, mirroring Akka/Pekko Streams Typed.
- [testkit](https://docs.rs/testkit/index.html)
- Stream testing probes built on Datum’s normal runtime.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Actor](https://docs.rs/struct.ActorRef.html)- Ref
- An [ActorRef](https://docs.rs/struct.ActorRef.html)is a strongly-typed wrapper over an[ActorCell](https://docs.rs/ractor/0.15.13/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/ractor/actor/actor_cell/struct.ActorCell.html)to provide some syntactic wrapping on the requirement to pass the actor’s message type everywhere.
- [Attributes](https://docs.rs/struct.Attributes.html)
- An ordered, immutable collection of `Attribute`

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Attribute](https://docs.rs/enum.Attribute.html)
- A single piece of stream/stage metadata.

# lellm - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/lellm/0.4.6/lellm/

## Expand description

LeLLM — Rust LLM orchestration framework.

默认开启 `provider`（core + provider 适配层）。

```
# 默认：core + provider
lellm = "0.2"
# 需要 Graph 编排层
lellm = { version = "0.2", features = ["graph"] }
# 需要 Agent 运行时
lellm = { version = "0.2", features = ["agent"] }
# 需要 MCP 协议
lellm = { version = "0.2", features = ["mcp"] }
# 全部启用
lellm = { version = "0.2", features = ["full"] }
```
## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use`- [lellm_provider](https://docs.rs/lellm-provider/0.4.5/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/lellm_provider/index.html)as provider;

---

# lellm_mcp - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/lellm-mcp/0.4.6/lellm_mcp/

## Expand description

lellm-mcp — MCP (Model Context Protocol) Client for LeLLM.

MVP 原型：验证接口冻结是否正确。

仅实现：stdio transport + tools/list + tools/call + initialize

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [checkpoint](https://docs.rs/checkpoint/index.html)
- 检查点 + 持久化 — Checkpoint, Policy, Codec, Store, MutationLog, Trace。
- [compiler](https://docs.rs/compiler/index.html)
- Compiler — 图优化 pass 框架。
- [error](https://docs.rs/error/index.html)
- Graph 错误类型。
- [event](https://docs.rs/event/index.html)
- Graph 层流式事件。
- [exec](https://docs.rs/exec/index.html)
- 执行引擎 — ExecutionEngine, ExecutionLoop, Session。
- [graph](https://docs.rs/graph/index.html)
- 图构建 — Graph, GraphBuilder, GraphAnalysis。
- [ids](https://docs.rs/ids/index.html)
- TraceId / SpanId — 执行追踪标识符。
- [node](https://docs.rs/node/index.html)
- 节点定义 — Node, Barrier, Parallel, Subgraph, Context。
- [runtime_](https://docs.rs/runtime_event/index.html)- event
- RuntimeEvent — Control Plane 控制面事件。
- [state](https://docs.rs/state/index.html)
- 状态管理 — State, WorkflowState, StateKey, StateLens。
- [stream_](https://docs.rs/stream_chunk/index.html)- chunk
- StreamChunk — Data Plane 数据面事件。
- [stream_](https://docs.rs/stream_emitter/index.html)- emitter
- StreamSink — 数据面发射抽象。
- [test_](https://docs.rs/test_executor/index.html)- executor
- 测试用执行器 — 替代已删除的 SimpleExecutor。

# lellm_derive - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/lellm-derive/0.4.6/lellm_derive/

## Expand description

lellm-derive — 派生宏与属性宏。

[§](https://docs.rs#%E4%B8%89%E7%BA%A7-api)三级 API

[§](https://docs.rs#level-1-tool-%E5%87%BD%E6%95%B0%E5%AE%8F%E6%8E%A8%E8%8D%9095-%E7%94%A8%E6%88%B7)Level 1: `#[tool]` 函数宏（推荐，95% 用户）

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use lellm_agent::ToolResult;
use lellm_derive::tool;
#[tool(name = "search", description = "搜索互联网信息")]
async fn search(query: String, limit: Option<u32>) -> ToolResult {
    // 实现逻辑
    Ok(format!("搜索结果: {}", query))
}
// 无依赖 — 直接调用生成的工厂函数：
builder.tool(search_tool());
// 有依赖 — 使用 _with 后缀工厂函数：
let client = SearchClient::new();
builder.tool(search_tool_with({
    let client = client.clone();
    move |args| async move {
        client.search(&args.query, args.limit).await
    }
}));
```
[§](https://docs.rs#level-2-derivetool-struct-%E5%AE%8F%E9%AB%98%E7%BA%A7%E7%94%A8%E6%88%B7)Level 2: `#[derive(Tool)]` struct 宏（高级用户）

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use lellm_agent::ToolResult;
use lellm_derive::Tool;
#[derive(Tool, JsonSchema)]
#[tool(name = "search", description = "搜索互联网信息")]
struct SearchArgs {
    /// 搜索关键词
    query: String,
    /// 返回数量
    limit: Option<u32>,
}
// 注册：
let reg = SearchArgs::safe(|args| async move {
    Ok(format!("搜索结果: {}", args.query))
});
```
[§](https://docs.rs#level-3-toolregistrationsafe%E6%A1%86%E6%9E%B6%E5%BC%80%E5%8F%91%E8%80%85)Level 3: `ToolRegistration::safe()`（框架开发者）

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use lellm_agent::{ToolDefinition, ToolRegistration};
let reg = ToolRegistration::safe(
    ToolDefinition {
        name: "search".to_string(),
        description: "搜索".to_string(),
        parameters: serde_json::json!({
            "type": "object",
            "properties": { "query": { "type": "string" } }
        }),
    },
    |args| async { Ok(args["query"].as_str().unwrap().to_string()) }
);
```

# mermaid_rs_renderer - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/mermaid-rs-renderer/0.3.0/mermaid_rs_renderer/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#mmdr---fast-mermaid-diagram-renderer)mmdr - Fast Mermaid Diagram Renderer

A pure Rust implementation of Mermaid diagram rendering, providing 100-600x faster rendering than mermaid-cli by eliminating browser dependencies.

[§](https://docs.rs#quick-start)Quick Start

```
use mermaid_rs_renderer::{render, render_with_options, RenderOptions};
let diagram = r#"
flowchart LR
    A[Start] --> B{Decision}
    B -->|Yes| C[OK]
    B -->|No| D[Cancel]
"#;
// Simple one-liner
let svg = render(diagram).unwrap();
// With options
let svg = render_with_options(diagram, RenderOptions::default()).unwrap();
```
[§](https://docs.rs#pipeline-control)Pipeline Control

For more control over the rendering pipeline, use the individual stages:

```
use mermaid_rs_renderer::{parse_mermaid, compute_layout, render_svg};
use mermaid_rs_renderer::{Theme, LayoutConfig};
let diagram = "flowchart LR; A-->B-->C";
// Stage 1: Parse
let parsed = parse_mermaid(diagram).unwrap();
// Stage 2: Layout
let theme = Theme::modern();
let config = LayoutConfig::default();
let layout = compute_layout(&parsed.graph, &theme, &config);
// Stage 3: Render
let svg = render_svg(&layout, &theme, &config);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#supported-diagram-types)Supported Diagram Types

- **Flowcharts**(- `flowchart`/- `graph`): TD, TB, LR, RL, BT directions
- **Sequence Diagrams**(- `sequenceDiagram`)
- **Class Diagrams**(- `classDiagram`)
- **State Diagrams**(- `stateDiagram-v2`)
- **ER Diagrams**(- `erDiagram`)
- **Pie Charts**(- `pie`)
- **XY Charts**(- `xychart`)
- **Quadrant Charts**(- `quadrantChart`)
- **Gantt**(- `gantt`)
- **Timeline**(- `timeline`)
- **Journey**(- `journey`)
- **Mindmap**(- `mindmap`)
- **Git Graph**(- `gitGraph`)

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

- Pure Rust, no browser or Node.js required
- ~3ms cold start vs ~2500ms for mermaid-cli
- ~15MB memory vs ~300MB for mermaid-cli
- SVG and PNG output (PNG via resvg)
- Customizable themes and layout configuration

[§](https://docs.rs#cargo-features)Cargo Features

- `cli`
- `png`

For minimal dependencies (e.g., embedding in other tools like Zola):

```
[dependencies]
mermaid-rs-renderer = { version = "0.2.2", default-features = false }
```

# trifle - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/trifle/0.5.0/trifle/

## Expand description

`trifle` — embedded, typo-tolerant trigram fuzzy search backed by SQLite.

trifle indexes short text segments and answers typo- and partial-tolerant queries, returning
matches that each carry where they matched. It owns a single SQLite store holding the segment
text, the caller key, and an inverted index (a base-plus-delta CRoaring posting per token),
and ranks by rarity-weighted shared-token overlap, counted bit-sliced in the
[ trifle_overlap](https://docs.rs/trifle-overlap/0.5.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/trifle_overlap/index.html) engine. The store is a derived, rebuildable cache over a caller-owned
source of truth; trifle never touches the caller’s data store.

It targets large corpora of small documents (≲ 1–2 KB per segment) read often and written infrequently. It is a fuzzy lexical overlap engine: rarer shared grams weigh more, and rarity is normalized per script class so a CJK bigram and a Latin trigram compare fairly. There is no BM25 or relevance tier.

[§](https://docs.rs#quick-start)Quick start

```
use trifle::{Config, Index, Schema, SearchOpts};
let dir = tempfile::tempdir().unwrap();
let index = Index::open_at(&dir.path().join("trifle.db"), Schema::flat(), Config::default())?;
// Writes go through a short-lived writer lease; commit makes them durable + visible.
let mut w = index.writer()?;
w.upsert(1, &[("front", "the quick brown fox")])?;
w.upsert(2, &[("front", "the quack brown ox")])?;
w.commit()?;
drop(w);
// Reads go through a reader lease. A typo'd query still matches.
let hits = index.reader()?.matches("quikc brown", &SearchOpts::new(), 10)?;
assert!(hits.iter().any(|m| m.key.as_i64() == Some(1)));
```
[§](https://docs.rs#the-data-model)The data model

A [ Schema](https://docs.rs/struct.Schema.html) declares a

**key**(its shape —

`Integer`/`Text`/`Blob`) plus named **text fields**. A

[is a](https://docs.rs/struct.Document.html)

`Document`[and a set of named segments (](https://docs.rs/enum.Key.html)

`Key``label → text`); a match
comes back as a [carrying the document key, the matched segment’s label, the matched byte span, and the segment’s text. There is no](https://docs.rs/struct.Match.html)

`Match``doc` table: the key lives directly on each
segment row.[§](https://docs.rs#the-read-surface)The read surface

[ Reader::matches](https://docs.rs/struct.Reader.html#method.matches) is the eager default: the top

`limit` hydrated matches.
[is the lazy spine: a best-first](https://docs.rs/struct.Reader.html#method.candidates)

`Reader::candidates`[of provenance-only](https://docs.rs/struct.CandidateStream.html)

`CandidateStream`[s that a caller composes reranking, pagination, or fusion over, hydrating only what it keeps. Filtering is the opt-in](https://docs.rs/struct.Candidate.html)

`Candidate`[over the caller’s live data.](https://docs.rs/struct.SqlFilter.html)

`SqlFilter`[§](https://docs.rs#ingest-and-maintenance)Ingest and maintenance

Writes are cheap (a small delta append) and visible after [ commit](https://docs.rs/struct.Writer.html#method.commit).

[folds pending deltas;](https://docs.rs/struct.Index.html#method.compact)

`compact`[is the signal that a compaction is due.](https://docs.rs/struct.Stats.html#structfield.delta_backlog)

`Stats::delta_backlog`[fully reindexes via an atomic shadow swap, which a tokenizer,](https://docs.rs/struct.Index.html#method.rebuild)

`rebuild``data_version`, or schema change requires (each drops the cache on open).## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [error](https://docs.rs/error/index.html)
- The crate error type.
- [store](https://docs.rs/store/index.html)
- Storage: the owned-sidecar SQLite store and how trifle’s tables are named.
- [tokenize](https://docs.rs/tokenize/index.html)
- Tokenization: the one strategy a caller may supply, the script-aware tokenizer trifle defaults to, and the plain fixed-width n-gram tokenizers for single-script corpora.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Candidate](https://docs.rs/struct.Candidate.html)
- A scored, provenance-only candidate: no text, which `CandidateStream::hydrate`
- [Candidate](https://docs.rs/struct.CandidateStream.html)- Stream
- A lazy, snapshot-pinned candidate cursor. Owns a pooled connection with a pinned read
transaction and the engine `Counter``Busy`
- [Compact](https://docs.rs/struct.CompactStats.html)- Stats
- What a `compact`
- [Config](https://docs.rs/struct.Config.html)
- Index configuration. Constructed with `Config::default``Config::new``#[non_exhaustive]`, so fields may be added in minor releases and struct-literal construction is unavailable.
- [Document](https://docs.rs/struct.Document.html)
- A document to index: a `Key``label → text`). Used by`rebuild``#[non_exhaustive]`: constructed with`Document::new`
- [Index](https://docs.rs/struct.Index.html)
- An embedded fuzzy-search index over text segments.
- [Match](https://docs.rs/struct.Match.html)
- One ranked match. Rank is conveyed by position in the returned `Vec<Match>`; the absolute relevance magnitude and the components it decomposes into ride along.
- [Reader](https://docs.rs/struct.Reader.html)
- A read lease: the surface for searches. The snapshot is per search or stream rather than per lease.
- [Schema](https://docs.rs/struct.Schema.html)
- A validated, immutable index schema.
- [Schema](https://docs.rs/struct.SchemaBuilder.html)- Builder
- Builder for a `Schema`
- [Search](https://docs.rs/struct.SearchOpts.html)- Opts
- Per-search options. Constructed with `SearchOpts::new``#[non_exhaustive]`, so struct-literal construction is unavailable.
- [SqlFilter](https://docs.rs/struct.SqlFilter.html)
- An opt-in raw-SQL filter: a trusted-constant predicate fragment over the `seg`columns (`id`,`key`,`label`,`txt`,`len`), or co-located caller tables via`ATTACH`, plus its bound params.
- [Stats](https://docs.rs/struct.Stats.html)
- A read-only snapshot of the index’s observable state.
- [Term](https://docs.rs/struct.Term.html)
- A packed term: a gram (≤3 codepoints) plus a script tag, `[ script:8 | c0:32 | c1:32 | c2:32 | reserved:24=0 ]`(MSB→LSB). Produced by`IntoTerm::term`
- [Tuning](https://docs.rs/struct.Tuning.html)
- The scoring and selection constants, grouped off `SearchOpts``None`selects the derived default. Constructed with`Tuning::new``docs/tuning.md`) describes what evaluation justifies changing each one.
- [Writer](https://docs.rs/struct.Writer.html)
- The exclusive write lease: holding it is holding the single-writer lock. One transaction is
open for the lease; `commit`

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Collapse](https://docs.rs/enum.Collapse.html)
- The retrieval granularity: what one result is, and therefore what `limit`counts.
- [Key](https://docs.rs/enum.Key.html)
- A caller key — the lifecycle handle trifle compares (dedup / replace / delete) and
returns on a match. Its `KeyShape``Schema`
- [KeyShape](https://docs.rs/enum.KeyShape.html)
- The declared shape of the `Key``seg.key`column type and settles comparability (native for int/text, memcmp for blob).

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Into](https://docs.rs/trait.IntoTerm.html)- Term
- Conversion of a gram-like value into its packed `Term``Borrow<str>`, so a string-backed tokenizer token gets it for free; the default derives the script and packs the gram’s code points. The`Tokenizer``&str`.

# sandpit - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sandpit/0.5.3/sandpit/

## Expand description

A concurrent, generational, trace and sweep garbage collected arena.

[§](https://docs.rs#creating-an-arena)Creating An Arena

All garbage collection in Sandpit happens within an arena. Therefore, to be begin we can start with creating a new arena.

This can be done like so..

```
use sandpit::{Arena, Root};
// This creates an arena with a `MyRoot` as the root.
let gc: Arena<Root![MyRoot]> = Arena::new(|mutator| {
    MyRoot::new(mutator)
});
```
There are two big things to unpack here:

- An `Arena`is generic on its single Root value which it holds.
- The Root of an `Arena`must be a Higher Kinded Type(HKT).

This is explained in much further depth in [ sandpit::Arena](https://docs.rs/struct.Arena.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#trace-trait)Trace Trait

For a type to be GC’ed it is required to impl [ Trace](https://docs.rs/trait.Trace.html)
which can be safely derived as long as all inner types also impl

[.](https://docs.rs/trait.Trace.html)

`Trace````
use sandpit::{Trace, Gc, GcOpt};
#[derive(Trace)]
enum Value<'gc> {
    // GC values must be branded with a mutation lifetime
    // to ensure freeing memory can happen safely.
    A(Gc<'gc, A>), // Mutable pointer to a garbage collected value
    B(GcOpt<'gc, B>), // Optionally null pointer that is also mutable. Can be unwrapped into a Gc.
}
// All inner values must be trace, therefore types A and B must impl Trace as well.
```
Essentially when a value is traced the tracer will mark the value as live, and call trace on all its inner pointers to GC values.

There are 2 types of GC pointers:

A type may also derive [ TraceLeaf](https://docs.rs/trait.TraceLeaf.html), if it contains no GC pointers.

[allows for easier interior mutability.](https://docs.rs/trait.TraceLeaf.html)

`TraceLeaf`[§](https://docs.rs#mutating-the-arena)Mutating the Arena

Once you have your arena and your traceable types, you can begin allocating
them in the arena by calling [ Arena::mutate](https://docs.rs/struct.Arena.html#method.mutate). Within a mutation
we can essentially do 3 important things:

- Access all data reaachable from the root.
- Create new garbage collected values.
- Update Gc pointers to point to new values via a `WriteBarrier`

```
use sandpit::{Trace, Gc};
arena.mutate(|mutator, root| {
    // We can access everything reachable from the root.
    traverse(root);
    // We can allocate new Gc values.
    // Here is a pointer, to a pointer, to a bool!
    let gc_mut = Gc::new(mutator,
        Gc::new(mutator, true)
    );
    // We can mutate existing inner Gc and GcOpt pointers.
    gc_mut.write_barrier(mutator, |barrier| {
        barrier.set(Gc::new(mutator, false));
    })
});
```
[§](https://docs.rs#collection-and-yielding)Collection and Yielding

In order for the Gc to free memory, and do so safely, all mutations must exit. Therefore, if a mutation involves a continuous loop of instructions, it must exit it’s mutation every so often to allow the GC to free memory.

The mutator exposes a signal([ Mutator::gc_yield](https://docs.rs/struct.Mutator.html#method.gc_yield)) which indicates if it is ready to free memory,
and that the mutation should end.

```
arena.mutate(|mutator, root| loop {
    // during this function it is likely the the GC will concurrently begin tracing!
    allocate_stuff(mutator, root);
    if mutator.gc_yield() {
        // the mutator is signaling to us that memory is ready to be freed so we should leave the mutation context
        break;
    } else {
        // if the mutator isn't signaling for us to yield then we
        // are fine to go on allocating more garbage
    }
});
```
* WARNING:* If a mutation continously runs without occasionally checking
the yield signal, memory cannot be freed!

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [Root](https://docs.rs/macro.Root.html)
- Re-exported from ForLt. Used in making the root of an arena.
Produce `impl`types[ForLt](https://docs.rs/trait.Root.html)*on demand*.
- [field](https://docs.rs/macro.field.html)
- Exists to allow getting a write barrier to an inner field.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Arena](https://docs.rs/struct.Arena.html)
- A concurrently garbage collected arena with a single root type.
- [Config](https://docs.rs/struct.Config.html)
- This structure contains the configuration settings for a garbage collector.
- [Gc](https://docs.rs/struct.Gc.html)
- Immutable Gc pointer, meaning a write barrier cannot be used to update this pointer.
- [GcOpt](https://docs.rs/struct.GcOpt.html)
- A GC pointer which is able of pointing to null.
- [GcVec](https://docs.rs/struct.GcVec.html)
- [Inner](https://docs.rs/struct.InnerBarrier.html)- Barrier
- [Metrics](https://docs.rs/struct.Metrics.html)
- A ‘snapshot’ of the metrics relevant to the GC’s internal triggers.
- [Mutator](https://docs.rs/struct.Mutator.html)
- Allows for allocation and mutation within the GC arena.
- [Tagged](https://docs.rs/struct.Tagged.html)
- [Write](https://docs.rs/struct.WriteBarrier.html)- Barrier
- Allows for the mutation of `Gc``GcOpt`

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [GcSync](https://docs.rs/trait.GcSync.html)
- [Root](https://docs.rs/trait.Root.html)
- Re-exported from ForLt. Used in making the root of an arena.
The main trait of the crate. The one expressing `: <'_>`-genericity.
- [Tag](https://docs.rs/trait.Tag.html)
- [Trace](https://docs.rs/trait.Trace.html)
- Allows tracer to find all GC references stored in a type.
- [Trace](https://docs.rs/trait.TraceLeaf.html)- Leaf
- Indicates a type contains no Gc references internally.

# async-dup 1.2.4 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/async-dup/1.2.4

# async-dup

Duplicate an async I/O handle.

This crate provides two tools, `Arc` and `Mutex`:

- `Arc`implements- `AsyncRead`,- `AsyncWrite`, and- `AsyncSeek`if a reference to the inner type does.
- A reference to `Mutex`implements`AsyncRead`,`AsyncWrite`, and`AsyncSeek`if the inner type does.

Wrap an async I/O handle in `Arc` or `Mutex` to clone it or share among tasks.

## Examples

Clone an async I/O handle:

```
use Arc;
use io;
use Async;
use TcpStream;
// A client that echoes messages back to the server.
let stream = connect.await?;
// Create two handles to the stream.
let reader = new;
let mut writer = reader.clone;
// Echo data received from the reader back into the writer.
copy.await?;
```
Share an async I/O handle:

```
use Mutex;
use io;
use *;
// Reads data from a stream and echoes it back.
async
```

at your option.

# async_dup - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/async-dup/1.2.4/target-redirect/async_dup/

## Expand description

Duplicate an async I/O handle.

This crate provides two tools, [ Arc](https://docs.rs/struct.Arc.html) and

[:](https://docs.rs/struct.Mutex.html)

`Mutex`- `Arc`- `AsyncRead`- `AsyncWrite`- `AsyncSeek`
- A reference to `Mutex``AsyncRead``AsyncWrite``AsyncSeek`

Wrap an async I/O handle in [ Arc](https://docs.rs/struct.Arc.html) or

[to clone it or share among tasks.](https://docs.rs/struct.Mutex.html)

`Mutex`[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

Clone an async I/O handle:

```
use async_dup::Arc;
use futures::io;
use smol::Async;
use std::net::TcpStream;
// A client that echoes messages back to the server.
let stream = Async::<TcpStream>::connect(([127, 0, 0, 1], 8000)).await?;
// Create two handles to the stream.
let reader = Arc::new(stream);
let mut writer = reader.clone();
// Echo data received from the reader back into the writer.
io::copy(reader, &mut writer).await?;
```
Share an async I/O handle:

```
use async_dup::Mutex;
use futures::io;
use futures::prelude::*;
// Reads data from a stream and echoes it back.
async fn echo(stream: impl AsyncRead + AsyncWrite + Unpin) -> io::Result<u64> {
    let stream = Mutex::new(stream);
    io::copy(&stream, &mut &stream).await
}
```
## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Arc](https://docs.rs/struct.Arc.html)
- A reference-counted pointer that implements async I/O traits.
- [Mutex](https://docs.rs/struct.Mutex.html)
- A mutex that implements async I/O traits.
- [Mutex](https://docs.rs/struct.MutexGuard.html)- Guard
- A guard that releases the mutex when dropped.

---

# Arc in async_dup - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/async-dup/1.2.4/async_dup/struct.Arc.html

# Struct Arc

[Source](../src/async_dup/lib.rs.html#74) `pub struct Arc<T>(pub `[Arc](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/sync/struct.Arc.html)<T>);

## Expand description

A reference-counted pointer that implements async I/O traits.

This is just a wrapper around `std::sync::Arc`

- `impl<T> AsyncRead for Arc<T> where &T: AsyncRead {}`
- `impl<T> AsyncWrite for Arc<T> where &T: AsyncWrite {}`
- `impl<T> AsyncSeek for Arc<T> where &T: AsyncSeek {}`

Constructs a new `Arc<T>`.

[§](#examples)Examples

```
use async_dup::Arc;
let a = Arc::new(7);
```

# Mutex in async_dup - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/async-dup/1.2.4/async_dup/struct.Mutex.html

`pub struct Mutex<T>(/* private fields */);`## Expand description

A mutex that implements async I/O traits.

This is a blocking mutex that adds the following impls:

- `impl<T> AsyncRead for Mutex<T> where T: AsyncRead + Unpin {}`
- `impl<T> AsyncRead for &Mutex<T> where T: AsyncRead + Unpin {}`
- `impl<T> AsyncWrite for Mutex<T> where T: AsyncWrite + Unpin {}`
- `impl<T> AsyncWrite for &Mutex<T> where T: AsyncWrite + Unpin {}`
- `impl<T> AsyncSeek for Mutex<T> where T: AsyncSeek + Unpin {}`
- `impl<T> AsyncSeek for &Mutex<T> where T: AsyncSeek + Unpin {}`

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/async_dup/lib.rs.html#258-260)#### pub fn [lock](https://docs.rs#method.lock)(&self) -> [MutexGuard](https://docs.rs/struct.MutexGuard.html)<'_, T>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/async_dup/lib.rs.html#258-260)

#### pub fn [lock](https://docs.rs#method.lock)(&self) -> [MutexGuard](https://docs.rs/struct.MutexGuard.html)<'_, T>

Acquires the mutex, blocking the current thread until it is able to do so.

Returns a guard that releases the mutex when dropped.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-1)Examples

```
use async_dup::Mutex;
let mutex = Mutex::new(10);
let guard = mutex.lock();
assert_eq!(*guard, 10);
```
Returns a mutable reference to the underlying data.

Since this call borrows the mutex mutably, no actual locking takes place – the mutable borrow statically guarantees the mutex is not already acquired.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-4)Examples

```
use async_dup::Mutex;
let mut mutex = Mutex::new(0);
*mutex.get_mut() = 10;
assert_eq!(*mutex.lock(), 10);
```
## Trait Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#trait-implementations)

# async_dup - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/async-dup/latest/async_dup/

## Expand description

Duplicate an async I/O handle.

This crate provides two tools, [ Arc](https://docs.rs/struct.Arc.html) and

[:](https://docs.rs/struct.Mutex.html)

`Mutex`- `Arc`- `AsyncRead`- `AsyncWrite`- `AsyncSeek`
- A reference to `Mutex``AsyncRead``AsyncWrite``AsyncSeek`

Wrap an async I/O handle in [ Arc](https://docs.rs/struct.Arc.html) or

[to clone it or share among tasks.](https://docs.rs/struct.Mutex.html)

`Mutex`[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

Clone an async I/O handle:

```
use async_dup::Arc;
use futures::io;
use smol::Async;
use std::net::TcpStream;
// A client that echoes messages back to the server.
let stream = Async::<TcpStream>::connect(([127, 0, 0, 1], 8000)).await?;
// Create two handles to the stream.
let reader = Arc::new(stream);
let mut writer = reader.clone();
// Echo data received from the reader back into the writer.
io::copy(reader, &mut writer).await?;
```
Share an async I/O handle:

```
use async_dup::Mutex;
use futures::io;
use futures::prelude::*;
// Reads data from a stream and echoes it back.
async fn echo(stream: impl AsyncRead + AsyncWrite + Unpin) -> io::Result<u64> {
    let stream = Mutex::new(stream);
    io::copy(&stream, &mut &stream).await
}
```
## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Arc](https://docs.rs/struct.Arc.html)
- A reference-counted pointer that implements async I/O traits.
- [Mutex](https://docs.rs/struct.Mutex.html)
- A mutex that implements async I/O traits.
- [Mutex](https://docs.rs/struct.MutexGuard.html)- Guard
- A guard that releases the mutex when dropped.

| Available RAM | 6.44 GB |

| Maximum size of a build log | 102.4 kB |
| Network access | blocked |
| Maximum number of build targets | 10 |

                    If a build fails because it hit one of those limits please
                    [open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose)
                    to get them increased.

# async-lock 3.4.2 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/async-lock/^3.1.0

# async-lock

Async synchronization primitives.

This crate provides the following primitives:

- `Barrier`- enables tasks to synchronize all together at the same time.
- `Mutex`- a mutual exclusion lock.
- `RwLock`- a reader-writer lock, allowing any number of readers or a single writer.
- `Semaphore`- limits the number of concurrent operations.

# futures-io 0.3.32 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/futures-io/^0.3.5

# futures-io

The `AsyncRead`, `AsyncWrite`, `AsyncSeek`, and `AsyncBufRead` traits for the futures-rs library.

## Usage

Add this to your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[]
 = "0.3"
```
The current `futures-io` requires Rust 1.36 or later.

## License

# futures 0.3.32 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/futures/^0.3.5

`futures-rs` is a library providing the foundations for asynchronous programming in Rust.
It includes key trait definitions like `Stream`, as well as utilities like `join!`,
`select!`, and various futures combinator methods which enable expressive asynchronous
control flow.

## Usage

Add this to your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[]
 = "0.3"
```
The current `futures` requires Rust 1.71 or later.

### Feature `std`

Futures-rs works without the standard library, such as in bare metal environments.
However, it has a significantly reduced API surface. To use futures-rs in
a `#[no_std]` environment, use:

```
[]
 = {  = "0.3",  = false }
```
## License

Licensed under either of [Apache License, Version 2.0](https://docs.rs/LICENSE-APACHE) or
[MIT license](https://docs.rs/LICENSE-MIT) at your option.

Unless you explicitly state otherwise, any contribution intentionally submitted for inclusion in the work by you, as defined in the Apache-2.0 license, shall be dual licensed as above, without any additional terms or conditions.

# smol 1.3.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/smol/^1

# smol

A small and fast async runtime.

This crate simply re-exports other smaller async crates (see the source).

To use tokio-based libraries with smol, apply the [ async-compat](https://docs.rs/async-compat) adapter to futures and I/O
types.

## Examples

Connect to an HTTP website, make a GET request, and pipe the response to the standard output:

```
use ;
```
There's a lot more in the [examples](https://github.com/smol-rs/smol/tree/master/examples) directory.

## Subcrates

- [async-channel](https://github.com/smol-rs/async-channel)- Multi-producer multi-consumer channels
- [async-executor](https://github.com/smol-rs/async-executor)- Composable async executors
- [async-fs](https://github.com/smol-rs/async-fs)- Async filesystem primitives
- [async-io](https://github.com/smol-rs/async-io)- Async adapter for I/O types, also timers
- [async-lock](https://github.com/smol-rs/async-lock)- Async locks (barrier, mutex, reader-writer lock, semaphore)
- [async-net](https://github.com/smol-rs/async-net)- Async networking primitives (TCP/UDP/Unix)
- [async-process](https://github.com/smol-rs/async-process)- Async interface for working with processes
- [async-task](https://github.com/smol-rs/async-task)- Task abstraction for building executors
- [blocking](https://github.com/smol-rs/blocking)- A thread pool for blocking I/O
- [futures-lite](https://github.com/smol-rs/futures-lite)- A lighter fork of- [futures](https://github.com/rust-lang/futures-rs)
- [polling](https://github.com/smol-rs/polling)- Portable interface to epoll, kqueue, event ports, and wepoll

## TLS certificate

Some code examples are using TLS for authentication. The repository
contains a self-signed certificate usable for testing, but it should **not**
be used for real-world scenarios. Browsers and tools like curl will
show this certificate as insecure.

In browsers, accept the security prompt or use `curl -k` on the
command line to bypass security warnings.

The certificate file was generated using
[minica](https://github.com/jsha/minica) and
[openssl](https://www.openssl.org/):

```
minica --domains localhost -ip-addresses 127.0.0.1 -ca-cert certificate.pem
openssl pkcs12 -export -out identity.pfx -inkey localhost/key.pem -in localhost/cert.pem
```
Another useful tool for making certificates is [mkcert](https://github.com/FiloSottile/mkcert).

## License

Licensed under either of

- Apache License, Version 2.0 ([LICENSE-APACHE](https://docs.rs/LICENSE-APACHE)or[http://www.apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0](http://www.apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0))
- MIT license ([LICENSE-MIT](https://docs.rs/LICENSE-MIT)or[http://opensource.org/licenses/MIT](http://opensource.org/licenses/MIT))

at your option.

# async-dup 1.2.3 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/async-dup/1.2.3

# async-dup

Duplicate an async I/O handle.

This crate provides two tools, `Arc` and `Mutex`:

- `Arc`implements- `AsyncRead`,- `AsyncWrite`, and- `AsyncSeek`if a reference to the inner type does.
- A reference to `Mutex`implements`AsyncRead`,`AsyncWrite`, and`AsyncSeek`if the inner type does.

Wrap an async I/O handle in `Arc` or `Mutex` to clone it or share among tasks.

## Examples

Clone an async I/O handle:

```
use Arc;
use io;
use Async;
use TcpStream;
// A client that echoes messages back to the server.
let stream = connect.await?;
// Create two handles to the stream.
let reader = new;
let mut writer = reader.clone;
// Echo data received from the reader back into the writer.
copy.await?;
```
Share an async I/O handle:

```
use Mutex;
use io;
use *;
// Reads data from a stream and echoes it back.
async
```
## License

Licensed under either of

- Apache License, Version 2.0 ([LICENSE-APACHE](https://docs.rs/LICENSE-APACHE)or[http://www.apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0](http://www.apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0))
- MIT license ([LICENSE-MIT](https://docs.rs/LICENSE-MIT)or[http://opensource.org/licenses/MIT](http://opensource.org/licenses/MIT))

at your option.

#### Contribution

Unless you explicitly state otherwise, any contribution intentionally submitted for inclusion in the work by you, as defined in the Apache-2.0 license, shall be dual licensed as above, without any additional terms or conditions.

# async_dup - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/async-dup

## Expand description

Duplicate an async I/O handle.

This crate provides two tools, [ Arc](https://docs.rs/struct.Arc.html) and

[:](https://docs.rs/struct.Mutex.html)

`Mutex`- `Arc`- `AsyncRead`- `AsyncWrite`- `AsyncSeek`
- A reference to `Mutex``AsyncRead``AsyncWrite``AsyncSeek`

Wrap an async I/O handle in [ Arc](https://docs.rs/struct.Arc.html) or

[to clone it or share among tasks.](https://docs.rs/struct.Mutex.html)

`Mutex`[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

Clone an async I/O handle:

```
use async_dup::Arc;
use futures::io;
use smol::Async;
use std::net::TcpStream;
// A client that echoes messages back to the server.
let stream = Async::<TcpStream>::connect(([127, 0, 0, 1], 8000)).await?;
// Create two handles to the stream.
let reader = Arc::new(stream);
let mut writer = reader.clone();
// Echo data received from the reader back into the writer.
io::copy(reader, &mut writer).await?;
```
Share an async I/O handle:

```
use async_dup::Mutex;
use futures::io;
use futures::prelude::*;
// Reads data from a stream and echoes it back.
async fn echo(stream: impl AsyncRead + AsyncWrite + Unpin) -> io::Result<u64> {
    let stream = Mutex::new(stream);
    io::copy(&stream, &mut &stream).await
}
```
## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Arc](https://docs.rs/struct.Arc.html)
- A reference-counted pointer that implements async I/O traits.
- [Mutex](https://docs.rs/struct.Mutex.html)
- A mutex that implements async I/O traits.
- [Mutex](https://docs.rs/struct.MutexGuard.html)- Guard
- A guard that releases the mutex when dropped.

#Version 1.2.4-Use the `async-lock` crate as the locking mechanism. (#14)
#Version 1.2.3-Remove the unnecessary `simple-mutex` dependency. (#10)
#Version 1.2.2-Fix typos in the docs.
#Version 1.2.1-Forbid unsafe code.
#Version 1.2.0-Make the inner `std::sync::Arc` public.
#Version 1.1.0-Implement `AsyncSeek` for `Arc`, `Mutex`, and `&Mutex`.
#Version 1.0.1-Fix failing tests.
#Version 1.0.0-Initial version

# async-dup 1.2.4 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/async-dup/latest/source/README.md

```
[![Build](https://github.com/smol-rs/async-dup/workflows/Build%20and%20test/badge.svg)](
https://github.com/smol-rs/async-dup/actions)
[![License](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-Apache--2.0_OR_MIT-blue.svg)](
https://github.com/smol-rs/async-dup)
[![Cargo](https://img.shields.io/crates/v/async-dup.svg)](
https://crates.io/crates/async-dup)
[![Documentation](https://docs.rs/async-dup/badge.svg)](
https://docs.rs/async-dup)
Duplicate an async I/O handle.
This crate provides two tools, `Arc` and `Mutex`:
* *
Wrap an async I/O handle in `Arc` or `Mutex` to clone it or share among tasks.
Clone an async I/O handle:
```rust
use async_dup::Arc;
use futures::io;
use smol::Async;
use std::net::TcpStream;
// A client that echoes messages back to the server.
let stream = Async::<TcpStream>::connect("127.0.0.1:8000").await?;
// Create two handles to the stream.
let reader = Arc::new(stream);
let mut writer = reader.clone();
// Echo data received from the reader back into the writer.
io::copy(reader, &mut writer).await?;
```
Share an async I/O handle:
```rust
use async_dup::Mutex;
use futures::io;
use futures::prelude::*;
// Reads data from a stream and echoes it back.
async fn echo(stream: impl AsyncRead + AsyncWrite + Unpin) -> io::Result<u64> {
}
```

at your option.
Unless you explicitly state otherwise, any contribution intentionally submitted
for inclusion in the work by you, as defined in the Apache-2.0 license, shall be
dual licensed as above, without any additional terms or conditions.
```

# async-lock 3.4.2 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/async-lock/3.4.2

# async-lock

Async synchronization primitives.

This crate provides the following primitives:

- `Barrier`- enables tasks to synchronize all together at the same time.
- `Mutex`- a mutual exclusion lock.
- `RwLock`- a reader-writer lock, allowing any number of readers or a single writer.
- `Semaphore`- limits the number of concurrent operations.

# event_listener - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/event-listener/^5.0.0/

## Expand description

Notify async tasks or threads.

This is a synchronization primitive similar to [eventcounts](https://www.1024cores.net/home/lock-free-algorithms/eventcounts) invented by Dmitry Vyukov.

You can use this crate to turn non-blocking data structures into async or blocking data
structures. See a [simple mutex](https://github.com/smol-rs/event-listener/blob/master/examples/mutex.rs) implementation that exposes an async and a blocking interface
for acquiring locks.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

Wait until another thread sets a boolean flag:

```
use std::sync::atomic::{AtomicBool, Ordering};
use std::sync::Arc;
use std::thread;
use std::time::Duration;
use std::usize;
use event_listener::{Event, Listener};
let flag = Arc::new(AtomicBool::new(false));
let event = Arc::new(Event::new());
// Spawn a thread that will set the flag after 1 second.
thread::spawn({
    let flag = flag.clone();
    let event = event.clone();
    move || {
        // Wait for a second.
        thread::sleep(Duration::from_secs(1));
        // Set the flag.
        flag.store(true, Ordering::SeqCst);
        // Notify all listeners that the flag has been set.
        event.notify(usize::MAX);
    }
});
// Wait until the flag is set.
loop {
    // Check the flag.
    if flag.load(Ordering::SeqCst) {
        break;
    }
    // Start listening for events.
    let mut listener = event.listen();
    // Check the flag again after creating the listener.
    if flag.load(Ordering::SeqCst) {
        break;
    }
    // Wait for a notification and continue the loop.
    listener.wait();
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

-
The `std`feature (enabled by default) enables the use of the Rust standard library. Disable it for`no_std`support.
-
The `critical-section`feature enables usage of the`critical-section``event-listener`for`no_std`platforms.
-
The `portable-atomic`feature enables the use of the`portable-atomic`

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Event](https://docs.rs/struct.Event.html)
- A synchronization primitive for notifying async tasks and threads.
- [Event](https://docs.rs/struct.EventListener.html)- Listener
- A guard waiting for a notification from an `Event`

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Into](https://docs.rs/trait.IntoNotification.html)- Notification
- A value that can be converted into a `Notification`
- [Listener](https://docs.rs/trait.Listener.html)
- A handle that is listening to an `Event`
- [Notification](https://docs.rs/trait.Notification.html)
- A notification that can be used to notify an `Event`

# event_listener_strategy - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/event-listener-strategy/^0.5.0/

## Expand description

A strategy for using the [`event-listener`] crate in both blocking and non-blocking contexts.

One of the stand-out features of the [`event-listener`] crate is the ability to use it in both
asynchronous and synchronous contexts. However, sometimes using it like this causes a lot of
boilerplate to be duplicated. This crate aims to reduce that boilerplate by providing an
[ EventListenerFuture](https://docs.rs/trait.EventListenerFuture.html) trait that implements both blocking and non-blocking functionality.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use event_listener_strategy::{
   event_listener::{Event, EventListener},
   EventListenerFuture, FutureWrapper, Strategy
};
use std::pin::Pin;
use std::task::Poll;
use std::thread;
use std::sync::Arc;
// A future that waits three seconds for an event to be fired.
fn wait_three_seconds() -> WaitThreeSeconds {
    let event = Event::new();
    let listener = event.listen();
    thread::spawn(move || {
        thread::sleep(std::time::Duration::from_secs(3));
        event.notify(1);
    });
    WaitThreeSeconds { listener: Some(listener) }
}
struct WaitThreeSeconds {
    listener: Option<EventListener>,
}
impl EventListenerFuture for WaitThreeSeconds {
    type Output = ();
    fn poll_with_strategy<'a, S: Strategy<'a>>(
        mut self: Pin<&mut Self>,
        strategy: &mut S,
        context: &mut S::Context,
    ) -> Poll<Self::Output> {
        strategy.poll(&mut self.listener, context)
    }
}
// Use the future in a blocking context.
let future = wait_three_seconds();
future.wait();
// Use the future in a non-blocking context.
futures_lite::future::block_on(async {
    let future = FutureWrapper::new(wait_three_seconds());
    future.await;
});
```
## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use`- [event_listener](https://docs.rs/event-listener/5.4.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/event_listener/index.html);

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [easy_](https://docs.rs/macro.easy_wrapper.html)- wrapper
- A wrapper around an `EventListenerFuture`

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Blocking](https://docs.rs/struct.Blocking.html)- `std`and non-- `target_family=wasm`
- A strategy that blocks the current thread until the event is signalled.
- [Future](https://docs.rs/struct.FutureWrapper.html)- Wrapper
- A wrapper around an `EventListenerFuture``Future`
- [NonBlocking](https://docs.rs/struct.NonBlocking.html)
- A strategy that uses polling to efficiently wait for an event.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Event](https://docs.rs/trait.EventListenerFuture.html)- Listener - Future
- A future that runs using the [`event-listener`] crate.
- [Strategy](https://docs.rs/trait.Strategy.html)
- A strategy for polling an `EventListenerFuture``EventListener`
